newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Spain seen cutting rates, question over size.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spain seen cutting rates, question over size.

text.p: The Bank of Spain seems sure to cut its key money market rate from 7.25 percent now the 1997 budget is out of the way, the only uncertainty is over the size of the reduction, analysts said on Wednesday.

Markets have taken into account a quarter-point cut in the rate ever since the German Bundesbank lowered its repo rate in August. Analysts now say anything less than a half-point cut could trigger a spate of profit-taking.

All economists polled by Reuters forecast the Spanish central bank would ease credit at its regular repurchase tender on Thursday. Six out of 10 predicted a 0.5 percentage point reduction while the other four saw a 0.25 point cut.
"The market is clearly betting on a cut, but isn't very sure how much (the Bank of Spain) will go for," said one analyst.

The Spanish central bank has maintained its money market rate at 7.25 percent since July 4, preferring not to move until after the budget, seen as the key to Spain's joining a single European currency in 1999.

The conservative government last Friday delivered an austere package aimed at cutting the budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) next year, opening the way for membership of Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU).
The market is now looking for a thumbs-up from the monetary authority, which strengthens the case for a half-point cut, some analysts said.

Secretary of State Cristobal Montoro said on Tuesday he was confident of a rate cut, echoing comments by Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato and Catalan President Jordi Pujol at the weekend, although none of them commented on the size.

Although the case seemed strong for a 50 basis point cut, some economists argued the central bank could offer a quarter-point cut now and save another until after September inflation data was announced on October 11.
The consumer price index came in lower than expected in August, rising 0.3 percent month-on-month for a 3.7 percent increase year-on-year.

"The market is discounting a 50 basis point cut, but in view of the Bank of Spain's policy of gradual easing, we think it will only lower by 25 basis points," said Juan Cebrian of Analistas Financieros Internacionales in Madrid.
"The Bank of Spain could cut rates again in the near future, for example if inflation moderates a little further," he added.
Leaving the rate unchanged would be badly received by the markets, who might perceive such a decision as a show of disapproval for the government's draft 1997 accounts.

"If it doesn't ease it will disappoint expectations in the sense that (it would be like saying) the budget is not credible, and from the point of view of markets it could be catastrophic," said Carmen Hernansanz, analyst at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
Nevertheless, she did not expect the Bank of Spain to be aggressive. "I'm leaning more towards 25 basis points," she said.
